title: Mara and Clover's Quiet Magic
markdown:
In the highlands, where mountains scrape the heavens and villages cling to crags like hardy goats, Witch Mara kept a cottage that smelled of rosemary and stardust. She was no cackling sorceress. Her magic was quiet competence. She brewed chamomile that could mend a frayed spirit, and mended ripped cloaks with threads that had seen moonlight. She could coax a stubborn oven to bake evenly. She could persuade a wilting herb to perk up. She had an almost uncanny knack for making things work.

Clover, her familiar, was a cat of sleek midnight fur and eyes like chips of emerald. He was not given to dramatic purrs or playful pounces. He observed. He sat on the highest available surface and surveyed the cottage like a miniature king on a velvety throne. A flick of his tail said more than a hundred yelps. He was Mara’s silent sounding board, and he used the position wisely.

The annual Cragtop Carnival posted its banners. At its heart: the Great Spell-Casting Contest. For years the contest had belonged to two spellcasters of considerable, if flamboyant, talent. Elara Swift’s spells shimmered with almost blinding brilliance. Padraig Thorne’s incantations were as precise as a clockmaker’s tick. They were rivals without malice, each unwaveringly certain of their own style. Elara favoured grand sweeping gestures that filled the sky with colour. Padraig preferred intricate geometric displays of pure magical energy.

Mara felt a stirring of interest. She did not seek grand accolades. She did appreciate a well-organised competition, and the prize — a year’s supply of the finest mountain honey — was not to be sniffed at. The thought of that golden nectar over warm scones bent her mouth into a small smile.

“Clover, my discerning friend,” she said, stirring a pot that swirled with a gentle inner luminescence, “I believe it is time we showed these young whippersnappers a thing or two about competence.”

Clover blinked slowly, which was agreement, then stretched, emerald eyes on the simmering pot as if flavour itself were a spell worth judging.

While Elara practised pyrotechnics in her back garden, setting off miniature suns that made the village dogs howl in confused awe, and Padraig perfected symmetrical illusions — three-dimensional snowflakes that melted on the air — Mara chose a humbler work. A charm to encourage hardy mountain flowers, even in unforgiving rocky soil. Not flashy. The sort of magic that whispered warmth against harsh wind.

She spent her days in the small garden, murmuring to stubborn buds, Clover supervising from a sun-drenched patch of moss. Sometimes he nudged a recalcitrant seedling with his nose, a feline blessing. One afternoon, transplanting forget-me-nots, a gust threatened her prepared soil. Mara flicked a tiny invisible shield. Clover, sensing her intent, let out a low resonant purr that seemed to anchor the air. She sat back on her heels then, and simply watched a cloud snag on a distant peak and tear itself slowly into blue. The contest could wait for the length of a cloud.

The contest day dawned crisp. Pine and woodsmoke. The square became a riot of crimson, gold, and azure banners snapping between stone buildings. Below, the cliffside market buzzed: carved wooden figures, woven woolens, a baker’s warm crusty loaves. The judges sat in dignified greys and browns, faces etched with mountain weather.

Elara and Padraig were already spectacle. Elara, in iridescent silks, conjured cascades of light that danced like captive rainbows. Children gasped. Padraig, hair perfectly gelled, robes the colour of midnight, wove solidified mist into impossible shapes that defied gravity. Mara stood at the edge of the crowd with her earthenware pot and felt, for a treacherous moment, that quiet competence looked a great deal like having brought the wrong thing.

“And now, for the scoring!” Padraig boomed, drawing a parchment and a quill that glowed, tip sharpened to a needle. “Elara, my dear, your light display was an eight. Technically flawless, but perhaps lacking a certain oomph.”

Elara’s headdress flashed. “Oomph? Padraig, your mist sculptures are admirable for their symmetry, but they lack the soul of true artistry. A seven. Predictable forms. Adequate execution.”

They had devised a tradition of awarding each other style points, competing to see whom the judges would praise most. Mara found it rather amusing, and also, as she stepped forward, rather loud.

She approached the judging circle with quiet grace. Clover trotted beside her, tail high, an elegant counterpoint to all that had shimmered. No silks. No angled illusions. Only a pot of what looked like ordinary garden soil.

“My humble offering,” she said, voice soft and clear, “is a charm for resilience. For the small things that bring joy to our lives.”

A few gentle words. Hands tracing simple patterns, like a painter sketching an outline. No thunder. No lightning. Not even a whisper of wind. Elara and Padraig exchanged a glance that had a hint of easy target in it.

“Well now,” Padraig began, quill poised, a slight smirk. “Economical, wouldn’t you say, Elara? A touch of brown. Very down-to-earth.”

“Understated,” Elara agreed, with feigned sympathy. “One might even say a tad boring. The lack of visual flair is quite remarkable. A four for effort. Perhaps a two for visual impact. One wonders if it holds any practical use beyond decoration.”

Mara did not flinch. She smiled the small knowing smile she used on ovens and wilting herbs. Perhaps they were right. A whisper against roars. She nodded to Clover, who settled at her feet, emerald gaze on the pot.

A soft green shoot emerged from the soil. Then another. Then another. Tiny sapphire-blue flowers, no bigger than dewdrops, unfurled, each a miniature marvel. A gentle sweet fragrance filled the air — spring itself, against the metallic tang of Elara’s lights and the sterile cool of Padraig’s mist.

Clover’s purr was a rumble of deep satisfaction, a feline endorsement that seemed to resonate with the blooming. The elders leaned forward. Stern faces softened. They inhaled.

Villagers gathered, drawn by scent and the quiet marvel. They saw not just flowers but the promise of weather turning, the steadfast beauty that survived wind. A young child reached out, finger hovering above a bloom, eyes wide. The perfume seemed to weave a spell of peace over the bustling market.

Elara’s scoring quill faltered. Padraig’s too. The applause was not for dazzle. It was for the thing that made people step closer instead of stepping back.

“Perhaps,” Elara whispered, uncharacteristically subdued, gaze on a particularly perfect sapphire bloom, “a four for visual impact was a tad harsh. The delicacy is quite something.”

Padraig cleared his throat, adjusting his midnight robes. “The economy of the spell certainly delivered. I find myself compelled to award bonus points for sheer unadulterated loveliness. And for the olfactory appeal, which my mist forms utterly lack.”

When the tally was announced, it was Mara who was declared victor. Not for the loudest spell, nor the most complex, but for the one that brought the most genuine smiles and the sweetest fragrance to Cragtop. The elders nodded in unison.

The village celebrated with shared laughter, warm mulled cider, and lanterns strung across the square. Mara, content with her honey and the quiet satisfaction of a job that had worked, set down a special dish of cream for Clover. He purred his approval in his own inimitable way, then claimed the highest crate in the square, a king surveying a carnival that had, for once, remembered how to be still.

The mountain wind took the scent of her flowers and carried it along the goat tracks, a blue sweetness caught in the banners, as ordinary and as lasting as a well-baked scone.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
